items.name: Bendy straw
clues: A little girl who couldn’t reach the top of her tall glass.
A sweet shop in San Francisco. Her father patented his idea in 1937.
Ridges let it bend over the edge of a glass without closing. He made the first one with a screw and some dental floss.
Almost everyone, but its very first sale, in 1947, was to a hospital.
Single-use plastic ones have been banned in the EU since 2021.
A straw with a bend in it.

items.name: Electric toothbrush
clues: At first, dentists mainly recommended it to patients who found it hard to move their hands and fingers well.
Switzerland, 1954.
A small motor moves the head, so your hand doesn’t have to do all the work.
Millions of people, twice a day, in the bathroom.
The first ones had a cable and plugged into the wall.
It buzzes while you clean your teeth.

items.name: Braille
clues: People who are blind or can’t see well.
Paris, in the 1820s. The inventor was only 15.
Six raised dots in different patterns, one pattern for each letter, read with the fingertips.
You can find it on medicine packets in the EU and next to the buttons in many lifts.
It grew out of a military code that soldiers could read in the dark without a light.
It’s named after its inventor, Louis, who lost his sight as a small child.

items.name: Audiobook
clues: Blind readers in the USA, in the 1930s.
The American Foundation for the Blind, which called them ‘Talking Books’.
Someone reads the whole book aloud, and you listen.
Commuters, joggers, people doing the washing-up, and anyone who wants a story at bedtime.
Some of the very first long-playing records (LPs) weren’t music: they were these, because speech sounded clear enough on them.
A book you listen to instead of reading.

items.name: Tactile paving
clues: A friend of the inventor who was losing his sight.
Japan: invented in 1965 and first laid outside a school for the blind in Okayama in 1967.
Raised bumps or lines that you can feel through your shoes or with a cane.
You walk over it on most train platforms in Germany.
In 2021 Google celebrated the inventor, Seiichi Miyake, with a Google Doodle.
The bumpy, usually white or yellow lines along the edge of train platforms.

items.name: Typewriter
clues: A friend of the inventor who had lost her sight and wanted to write her own letters.
Italy, in the early 1800s. Some of the letters she wrote with it still exist.
You press a key and a letter is printed on the paper. The inventor also came up with carbon paper for the ink.
Writers and offices for over a hundred years. Today mostly collectors and fans of vintage things.
The letter layout on your laptop keyboard (QWERTZ in Germany) comes from it.
A machine you type on that prints straight onto paper: clack, clack, ding!
